narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 52.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is just over 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Being in the second decile, noticeably below the average of accepted students (around the sixth decile), signaled that your performance placed you near the bottom of your class, which the model associates with higher risk of struggling on the bar exam.

Your first-year class rank was the next most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure. Placing in the third decile, compared with an average of sixth decile among accepted applicants, reinforced the pattern of lower relative standing.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 3.30 it sits slightly above the 3.23 average of accepted students, so the model viewed this as a modest positive signal that slightly lowered the predicted risk of failure. However, this encouraging factor was not strong enough to outweigh the two class-rank indicators.

Your LSAT score of 36.5, family income in the upper-middle bracket, gender, race, and plan to attend full-time played little or no role in the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic standing in law school and consider targeted bar-preparation resources that address the specific demands measured by your lower class ranks. Reapplying with a stronger upper-year record could meaningfully change the prediction. (248 words)
